925.title: Ibn al-Haytham
925.hook: who showed that we see because light enters the eye, and tested ideas by experiment
925.howItsDone: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics argued from experiment that light enters the eye, and his doubts about Ptolemy urged seekers to test even the most respected books.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Biruni measures the earth: a mountain, one small angle, and a book on India written in its own words. Your line was: measure carefully. What did you check before you said it? Day nine hundred twenty-five.

Close your eyes for a moment, then open them. Did something go out of your eyes to reach the world, or did the world come in? For a long time, serious thinkers argued that the eye sends out rays, like a lamp, and touches what it sees. A scholar in Cairo set out to settle it. There is a story told about how he came to have the time. He had boasted that he could tame the flooding of the Nile, the caliph called him to do it, and when he saw it couldn't be done, he is said to have pretended to be mad to escape the ruler's anger, and spent a long time shut away, writing. Whether that's how it happened or not, the writing survives. His name was Ibn al-Haytham.
screen: `DO THE EYES SEND OUT RAYS?` → `A BOAST ABOUT THE NILE.` → `SHUT AWAY, WRITING.`

segments.voice: His great work is the Book of Optics, Kitab al-Manazir. His answer to the old question was clear: we see because light comes from things into the eye, not because the eye sends something out. Look at the sun and your eyes hurt. That is light coming in. But the more important thing is how he argued it. He didn't just reason. He set up tests. Take a dark room with a small hole in one wall, and set several lamps outside it. On the wall inside, a separate spot of light appears for each lamp. Cover one lamp, and its spot vanishes, while the others stay. So light travels in straight lines, and each source sends its own. Try it, change one thing, watch what happens. He had a word for this kind of careful checking, i'tibar. And he applied the same honesty to books. In a work of doubts about the great astronomer Ptolemy, he wrote that the person who seeks the truth should not simply trust the writings of the ancients, however famous. The seeker should question what he reads, test it from every side, and suspect even himself as he does, so he is not fooled by his own wishes. Muslim scholars before him had heard the Qur'an call them to look: at the sky, at the earth, at the night and the day, as signs for people who reflect. Ibn al-Haytham looked, and then built a room to check what he saw. Test it.
screen: `LIGHT COMES INTO THE EYE.` · `A DARK ROOM AND SOME LAMPS.` · `DON'T SIMPLY TRUST THE ANCIENTS.` · `SUSPECT EVEN YOURSELF.` · then, large: `TEST IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: test one assumption. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're sure of about your day or the people in it. That a coworker doesn't like you. That a task will take forever. That a friend is too busy to hear from you. Breathe in. Hold it up like a lamp outside the dark room. Breathe out. How could you check it, simply, today? One question, one try, one small experiment. Then suspect yourself a little, as Ibn al-Haytham said. If you pray, you can ask God to show you things as they are. If you don't, just stay curious. The bell holds the time.
Ibn al-Haytham. A scholar in Cairo who showed by experiment that light comes into the eye, and told seekers to question even the ancients, and themselves. Today's word.
Your line: test it. Today, take the assumption you picked and run the small experiment. Then notice what you learned. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

926.title: The astrolabe
926.hook: an instrument to find time, direction and the qiblah by the stars
926.howItsDone: Muslims pray at set times and face the Kaaba in Makkah, and astrolabes, along with the work of mosque timekeepers, were used to find the hour and the qiblah from the sun and stars.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn al-Haytham: a dark room, a few lamps, and light coming into the eye. Your line was: test it. Which assumption did you test, and what happened? Day nine hundred twenty-six.

It's night in a desert town. No clock on the wall, no phone in a pocket. A man steps into the courtyard holding a disk of brass, hung from a ring on his thumb. He lifts it to his eye, sights a bright star along a little bar on the back, and reads a mark on the rim. Then he turns the disk over and rotates a lacy brass cutout on the front until that star's pointer sits at the height he just read. And now he can read the hour. He can tell which way is north, and which way faces Makkah. A whole sky, folded into his hand. It is called the astrolabe.
screen: `A BRASS DISK ON A THUMB RING.` → `SIGHT A STAR.` → `READ THE HOUR.`

segments.voice: The astrolabe is older than Islam; Greek writers described it. But in the Muslim world it was refined, written about and made beautiful. Here's how it works, in plain terms. On the back is a sighting bar. You use it to measure how high the sun or a star stands above the horizon. On the front is a plate engraved with lines for the latitude where you live, and over it turns an open brass web, often called in Arabic al-ankabut, the spider, with little pointers for bright stars. Set the spider so your star sits at the height you just measured, and the instrument shows you the time, and where the sky will be. The Qur'an says that God has set the stars for people so they may guide their way by them in the darkness of land and sea. For people who pray at set times and face the Kaaba in Makkah when they pray, that guidance mattered every single day. Some mosques kept a timekeeper, called the muwaqqit, whose work was to find the times of prayer from the sun and the stars. And makers took pride in the craft. Ibn al-Nadim, writing a catalog of books and scholars in Baghdad, names an astrolabe maker of Aleppo, a woman called al-Ijliya, who worked for its ruler. The brass is engraved with star names, some of them Arabic, and some of those names still sit on our star maps. The stars tell the time, if you know how to read them.
screen: `OLDER THAN ISLAM, REFINED IN IT.` · `THE SIGHTING BAR AND THE SPIDER.` · `STARS SET FOR GUIDANCE.` · `THE TIMEKEEPER AND THE MAKERS.` · then, large: `THE STARS TELL THE TIME.`

segments.voice: The practice: find north. Settle, and breathe. If you know which way north is from where you're sitting, turn your face toward it now. If you don't, guess, and later check with a compass or the night sky. Breathe in. Feel the directions around you, north, east, south, west, as if you were standing in that courtyard with the brass disk. Breathe out. Tonight, if the sky is clear, step outside and look up for one minute. If you pray, you can bring to mind the direction you face in prayer. If you don't, just let the sky be big. The bell holds the time.
The astrolabe. A brass disk that measures the height of a star and turns it into the hour, the direction, and the qiblah. Today's word.
Your line: the stars tell the time. Today, look for the sun or the stars once, and guess the time before you check a clock. Day nine hundred twenty-six.

927.title: Why they studied the sky
927.hook: prayer times, the qiblah and the new moon made astronomy a devotion
927.howItsDone: Muslims begin Ramadan and the other months by the new crescent, set prayer times by the sun's position, and face the qiblah toward Mecca; communities differ on whether the crescent must be seen locally or may be accepted from elsewhere or by calculation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the astrolabe: a brass instrument for finding the hour and the direction of prayer by the stars. Your line was: the stars tell the time. Did you find north last night? Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

The prayers come through the day, but when, exactly? Not by a clock on the wall. By the sun. The Qur'an puts it plainly, in Pickthall's translation: "worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." Fixed hours, read from shadows, from sunset, from the last light in the west. Then a direction to face, from wherever you happen to be standing. Then a month that begins only when someone sees a thin crescent after sunset. Questions about the sky, and not idle ones. They come from the prayer mat and the fast.
screen: `WORSHIP AT FIXED HOURS.` → `A DIRECTION TO FACE.` → `A MONTH THAT STARTS WITH A CRESCENT.`

segments.voice: Start with the moon. People asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about the new moons, and the Qur'an answers, in Pickthall's words: "They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage." The crescent opens each month, so it opens Ramadan, the pilgrimage season and the feasts. Bukhari records the Prophet's instruction: fast when you see it, stop fasting when you see it again, and if clouds hide it, complete the month as thirty days. The calendar rests on a human eye, looking west at dusk. Then the direction. The Qur'an tells believers to turn their faces toward the Sacred Mosque wherever they are. Near Mecca, you can almost point. Far away, on a round earth, finding that line takes geometry: angles, distances, the shape of the globe. Then the hours. Tirmidhi records a report in which the angel Gabriel leads the Prophet in prayer at set moments: when the sun passes its height, when a shadow has grown, when the sun goes down, when the twilight fades. Every one of those is something you see in the sky or on the ground. So the sky became homework. The astrolabe makers you met yesterday were working on questions that started at the mosque door. And the conversation hasn't stopped. Muslims today settle the new moon in more than one way: some communities wait for a sighting in their own sky, some accept a sighting from another country, and some rely on calculation. Each reads the Prophet's instruction in its own way, and each is trying to keep the same fast. Science for prayer.
screen: `FIXED SEASONS FOR MANKIND.` · `TURN YOUR FACE, WHEREVER YOU ARE.` · `SHADOWS AND SUNSETS MARK THE HOURS.` · `ONE HADITH, SEVERAL WAYS TO SIGHT.` · then, large: `SCIENCE FOR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to watch for the new moon. Settle, and breathe. A new crescent shows low and thin in the sky where the sun has just gone down, in the short while after sunset. Make a note to find out what time the sun sets where you are tonight, so you know when to look. For now, notice the light where you are right now: how bright it is, which way the shadows fall, how long they are. People read the hour from exactly that. If you pray, you can let this quiet be part of waiting for the next prayer. If you don't, just keep watching the light. The bell holds the time.
Why they studied the sky. Prayer times, the direction of prayer and the new moon: questions from worship that sent people to the stars. Today's word.
screen: `WHY THEY STUDIED THE SKY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: science for prayer. Today, step outside once around sunset and look west, even for ten seconds, and see what the sky is doing. Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

928.title: Al-Jahiz and the animals
928.hook: the witty writer of the Book of Animals
928.howItsDone: The Qur'an speaks of animals among the signs of God, and al-Jahiz's Book of Animals is read today for its observation, its humor and its Arabic prose.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why they studied the sky: prayer times, the direction of prayer and the new moon sent people to the stars. Your line was: science for prayer. Did you look west at sunset? Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

Dog or rooster: which is the better creature? It sounds like an argument from the back of a school bus. In the Abbasid age, a writer from Basra put that argument into a huge book and let it run. The dog's champion speaks. The rooster's champion answers. Each brings poems, proverbs, stories from hunters, and things he has watched with his own eyes. And somewhere in the middle, the reader realizes this isn't really a book about winning. It's a book about looking. The writer was Amr ibn Bahr of Basra, and people knew him by a nickname: al-Jahiz.
screen: `DOG OR ROOSTER?` → `EACH SIDE MAKES ITS CASE.` → `A BOOK ABOUT LOOKING.`

segments.voice: The nickname, tradition says, was about his eyes, which bulged. He seems to have taken it with a grin, because wit runs through everything he wrote. He also wrote a whole book of stories about misers, people so tight-fisted the stories still get laughs. But his great sprawling work is the Kitab al-Hayawan, the Book of Animals. Open it anywhere and you find ants carrying grain, flies, mosquitoes, camels, dogs, birds, snakes. Next to them, a line of poetry about the same creature, a verse of the Qur'an, a tale a sailor told, and then al-Jahiz telling you which parts he believes and which he doesn't. Why spend a life on gnats and roosters? The Qur'an itself points at animals. In Pickthall's translation: "There is not an animal in the earth, nor a flying creature flying on two wings, but they are peoples like unto you." Peoples. Communities with their own ways. And elsewhere it asks, "Will they not regard the camels, how they are created?" For a reader like al-Jahiz, looking closely at a creature was a way of reading signs of the One who made it. So the smallest thing deserved a careful look, and a second look, and a joke along the way. That's the spirit of the whole book: nothing is too small or too strange to wonder about. The ant counts. The mosquito counts. The argument between the dog lover and the rooster lover counts, because both of them had to look hard to make their case. Curious about everything.

segments.voice: The practice: look closely at one animal. Settle, and breathe. If there's a creature near you, a pet, a bird at the window, a fly on the glass, a spider in the corner, watch it. If not, bring one to mind that you've seen today or this week. Notice how it moves. What it seems to want. How it uses its legs, or wings, or tail. What it does when it's still. Don't name it or judge it. Just look, the way al-Jahiz looked, as if it were a whole people with its own ways. If you pray, you can let the looking be a kind of thanks. If you don't, let it be plain attention. The bell holds the time.
Al-Jahiz and the animals. The witty writer of Basra whose Book of Animals mixes what he watched, what he heard, poetry and the Qur'an. Today's word.
Your line: curious about everything. Today, ask one question about something you normally walk straight past, and look for the answer. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

929.title: The booksellers' street
929.hook: Baghdad's book market, copyists and public libraries
929.howItsDone: Muslims honor the pen and the written word, and some mosques, schools and Islamic centers today keep libraries open to readers, continuing an old tradition of shared books.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Jahiz and his Book of Animals: dogs, roosters, ants and camels, all worth a careful look. Your line was: curious about everything. What did you stop and wonder about? Day nine hundred twenty-nine.

A blank sheet of paper, a reed pen, a pot of ink. Now line a street with them. Shop after shop, and in each one a person bent over a page, copying a book letter by letter while customers wander in to browse, haggle, argue about poetry, or sit down and read. In Abbasid Baghdad, the people who ran these shops had a name, warraq, and their market was known as the market of the warraqs. Before the printing press, this was how a book multiplied: one careful hand at a time.
screen: `A SHEET, A PEN, A POT OF INK.` → `SHOP AFTER SHOP OF COPYISTS.` → `ONE CAREFUL HAND AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Warraq is built on waraq, a leaf, a sheet of paper. So a warraq is a paper person: a copyist, a stationer, a bookseller, often all three. Some were hired hands. Some were scholars themselves, who copied books they loved and sold copies to pay the rent. One bookseller's son in Baghdad did something remarkable with the trade: Ibn al-Nadim, the same man whose catalogue gave us the astrolabe maker al-Ijliya three days ago. He wrote the Fihrist, the Catalogue: a list of books and their authors, across grammar, poetry, law, the Qur'an's sciences, philosophy, medicine, even the beliefs of other peoples. It reads like a walk down the shelves of his world, and it preserves the names of books that are now lost. Why did people care so much about pages? By the usual account, the first words revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, begin with a command to read, and go on, in Pickthall's translation: "Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not." The pen sits right there in the opening of the revelation. And around the shops there were libraries: collections in mosques, in schools, in the homes of patrons who opened their doors to readers. A student without money for a copy could still find a book to sit with. So walk the street again. Ink on fingers. Paper stacked in bundles. Someone reading aloud from a new copy to see if it sounds right. A city where a book was a thing you could walk to. The street of books.

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to visit a library. Settle, and breathe. If there's a book within reach, pick it up and hold it. Feel its weight, the edges of its pages. If there isn't, bring to mind a library you know, or one you've never been inside but could find. Think of the hands that made the book possible: the writer, whoever copied or printed it, whoever carried it to the shelf. Then pick a day this week when you could walk into a library, even for ten minutes, just to be among the shelves. If you pray, you can let this minute be thanks for the pen. If you don't, let it be thanks for the people who kept the pages. The bell holds the time.

930.title: Al-Bukhari's journey
930.hook: al-Bukhari travels for years, sifting hundreds of thousands of reports to compile his Sahih
930.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims read and teach Sahih al-Bukhari as a trusted collection of the Prophet's sayings, and students still learn to examine a report's chain of narrators; Shia Muslims rely on their own hadith collections and methods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the booksellers' street: copyists bent over pages, a bookseller's catalogue, libraries open to readers. Your line was: the street of books. Did you find your nearest library? Day nine hundred thirty.

A great book of reports about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, could have opened with a miracle, or a battle, or a law. This one opens with a sentence about the inside of a person. The Prophet says that actions are judged by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. That's the first report in the Sahih of al-Bukhari. Before a single rule about prayer or trade, the reader is asked: why are you doing this? It's a fitting door, because the man who built the book spent his life on a hard question of his own, and on the road to answer it.
screen: `A BOOK THAT OPENS WITH INTENTION.` → `WHY ARE YOU DOING THIS?` → `A MAN WITH A HARD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: His name was Muhammad ibn Isma'il, called al-Bukhari after Bukhara, the city he came from. His question was simple to say and hard to answer: did the Prophet really say this? A hadith is a report, and each one comes with a chain of people: I heard it from her, who heard it from him, who heard it from a companion of the Prophet. Al-Bukhari traveled from city to city to meet the people who carried those chains. Then he tested every link. Did these two people actually meet? Was each one honest? Was each one careful, with a strong memory? One weak link, and the report didn't go into his book, however lovely its words. The Qur'an gives the instinct behind it. In Pickthall's translation: "If an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it." Verify. Don't pass on what you haven't checked. Tradition says he heard a vast number of reports and kept only a small share, and that before writing each one down he would wash and pray. The result is the Sahih, which means sound. For Sunni Muslims it holds a place of deep trust, often named together with the collection of his student, Muslim. Shia Muslims also hold the Prophet's words in deep trust, and gather and weigh reports through their own collections and scholars, especially those passed down through the Prophet's family. Both care about the same thing: that what's said in the Prophet's name is really his. Sifted with care.
screen: `DID HE REALLY SAY THIS?` · `TEST EVERY LINK IN THE CHAIN.` · `IF AN EVIL-LIVER BRING YOU TIDINGS, VERIFY.` · `SAHIH MEANS SOUND.` · then, large: `SIFTED WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: The practice: check a source. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you heard or read this week and simply believed. A headline, a health tip, something a friend said about someone else. Now trace the chain, the way al-Bukhari would. Who told you? Where did they get it? Did they see it, or hear it from someone? Is there a link you can't see? You don't have to decide it's false. Just notice where your knowing stops. If you pray, you can ask for help to speak only what's true. If you don't, just hold the question: how do I know? The bell holds the time.

931.title: The great imams' age
931.hook: Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad teach in this age, and Ja'far al-Sadiq before them
931.howItsDone: The Sunni schools of law are the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali, and Twelver Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school; in daily practice people often learn their school's rulings from a local scholar or imam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Bukhari's journey: every chain of reports tested, link by link. Your line was: sifted with care. What did you check before passing it on? Day nine hundred thirty-one.

A teacher in Medina sits with a circle of students. In the circle, the biographies say, are two men who will each become the name of a whole way of practicing Islam. The teacher is Ja'far al-Sadiq, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, through Husayn. The students, tradition says, include Abu Hanifa of Kufa and Malik of Medina. Hold that picture: one circle, and in it names that Muslims still live by. When someone says they follow a Hanafi or Maliki or Ja'fari school, they're pointing back to rooms like this one.
screen: `ONE CIRCLE IN MEDINA.` → `JA'FAR AL-SADIQ TEACHES.` → `BRANCHES MUSLIMS STILL LIVE BY.`

segments.voice: Imam here means a leading scholar, someone others follow in prayer and in law. Shia Muslims honor Ja'far al-Sadiq as one of the Imams of the Prophet's family, and a Shia school of law carries his name: Ja'fari. Then the line of teachers runs on. Abu Hanifa, in Kufa, taught by discussion, turning cases over with his students, reasoning carefully where no text spoke directly. Malik, in Medina, gathered the hadith and the living practice of the Prophet's city into a book, the Muwatta. Al-Shafi'i studied with Malik, the biographies say, then traveled and wrote about how law should be drawn from the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Ahmad ibn Hanbal studied with al-Shafi'i, gathered a great collection of reports, and held to his convictions when the authorities pressured scholars to agree with them. Teacher to student to teacher. The Sunni schools carry their names: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali. These schools reach different answers on a range of questions: where to hold your hands in prayer, details of fasting and trade. The imams themselves knew it, and the stories about them are often stories of respect across the differences. A story people tell: a caliph wanted to make Malik's book the one law for every city. Malik said no. The companions of the Prophet, he said, had spread to many lands, each carrying knowledge, and people should be left with what had reached them. This week has walked through stars, light, animals, books and chains of reports. Today it reaches the teachers whose schools of law Muslims still follow. The age of the imams.
screen: `JA'FAR AL-SADIQ, AND THE JA'FARI SCHOOL.` · `ABU HANIFA REASONS, MALIK GATHERS.` · `AL-SHAFI'I, THEN AHMAD.` · `DIFFERENT ANSWERS, MUTUAL RESPECT.` · then, large: `THE AGE OF THE IMAMS.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a teacher. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who taught you how to do something right: a rule, a craft, a way of behaving. A parent, a coach, a teacher who explained things patiently, someone who showed you how a thing is properly done. Then think back past them: who taught them? And who taught that person? Let the chain go back as far as you can imagine it. If you pray, you can remember them, and their teachers, in your prayer. If you don't, just hold them in mind with thanks. Then picture how you'd tell them, if you could. The bell holds the time.
